data.title: Louisiana AG calls CFTC chair an ‘obsequious standard bearer’ for prediction markets following agency lawsuit
data.description:
Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill accused Commodity Futures Trading Commission Chairman Michael Selig of making "flatly false statements" on Saturday, a day after the agency sued the state to block a court order shutting prediction markets out of Louisiana.

"Flatly false statements by the 'obsequious standard bearer' for Kalshi and prediction markets. Gambling has been regulated by states for 250 years," Murrill wrote on X at 12:05 p.m. ET.

Murrill was replying to a Friday evening post in which Selig said event contracts "have traded openly in Louisiana for years, in compliance with the CEA and [CFTC] regulations." He called the state's "eleventh-hour 'emergency' lawsuit" against the industry "naked lawfare and a cynical political stunt."

CFTC sued to block statewide prediction market freeze

The CFTC and the United States filed a complaint in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana on Friday, naming the state, Murrill, the Louisiana Gaming Control Board and the state police's gaming enforcement division as defendants. The agency is asking the court to declare that state gambling laws are preempted for CFTC-regulated markets and to bar Louisiana from enforcing or extending the state court's order.

"The Commission's lawsuit seeks to maintain the status quo while the federal courts decide this issue in an orderly manner," Selig said in a statement. The agency said Louisiana is the 12th state it has sued to defend its claimed exclusive jurisdiction over derivatives markets.

On Thursday, the CFTC and the Justice Department also sued Arkansas to block its enforcement action against Kalshi. Selig told a conference audience on Friday that states were "essentially trying to lock up founders and CEOs" of prediction market companies, The Block reported.

Order covers 31 entities

Judge Jeffrey Johnson of the 21st Judicial District Court in Tangipahoa Parish signed the ex parte temporary restraining order Thursday afternoon, according to a copy Murrill posted on X. Murrill sued the companies earlier that day, making Louisiana the 11th state to sue one or more prediction markets.

The order names 31 entities tied to Kalshi, Polymarket, Robinhood, Crypto.com, Coinbase, Gemini, Interactive Brokers' ForecastEx, Novig, Underdog, IG Group and ProphetX. It bars them from offering event contracts on sports, elections, awards and other events to people in Louisiana without a state license, and requires them to geofence the state.

The order expires after 10 days unless the court extends it. A hearing on the state's motion for a preliminary injunction is set for 9 a.m. local time on Nov. 30.

Kalshi has cut off access for Louisiana users. A message in its app, seen in a screenshot reviewed by The Block, tells them, "Your government says you can't use Kalshi anymore," and says the state acted "without a hearing, notice, or due process." The screen includes a link reading "Protect your freedom to trade" and a button to "Join the movement."

The Block has reached out to Kalshi, Polymarket and Murrill's office for comment.

data.title: SpaceX's S&P 500 bid gets new life as Elon Musk pitches Tesla merger
data.description:
New Delhi, Nov. 14 -- Just months after SpaceX was denied a swift entry into the S&P 500 Index, Elon Musk may have found a backdoor: Merging with Tesla Inc., one of the stock-market benchmark's biggest members.

Talks have been progressing toward a tie-up that would consolidate Musk's business empire into a single behemoth spanning from electric cars and AI to satellite launches and social media. A main motivation would almost certainly be unleashing potential synergies as he seeks to push into expensive and speculative ventures like robotic assistants, orbital datacenters and even colonies on Mars.

But possible inclusion in the S&P 500 offers another significant incentive to a man whose nearly $900 billion fortune has relied heavily on salesmanship and a cult-like following among Tesla and SpaceX investors. That's because it would ensure that $16 trillion of passive index-tracking funds hold on to shares of the combined company, regardless of what happens to the outlook or the bottom line.

"If you hold an S&P index fund or ETF in your 401(k) or investment account, the manager of that fund is compelled to buy every stock in the index in proportion to its weight," said Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers. "As a result, you own all those stocks whether you knowingly intended to or not."

Both Tesla and SpaceX have been burning through billions of dollars in cash, and plan to bleed through more to finance new ventures, even as worries about the sustainability of the AI boom drag on the stock market.

While SpaceX reported its first quarter of positive earnings last month, Tesla has faced inconsistent demand for its cars in the US and mounting competition abroad. It just discontinued the Cybertruck, which became a divisive symbol of Musk's right-wing politics as he became a key adviser to US President Donald Trump after his return to the White House.

The stocks also hover at particularly lofty levels. Even after slipping 13% this year, Tesla is trading at more than 180 times its expected earnings, compared with 18 for the overall S&P 500. Soon after its initial public offering in June, SpaceX commanded a market value of as much as $2.6 trillion, a heady level for a company that had $32 billion in revenue in the 12 months through September.

In the face of that record-setting IPO, Nasdaq changed its rules to speed the company's entrance into the Nasdaq 100 Index, which is tracked by about $800 billion in assets.

But S&P Dow Jones Indices went the opposite route, opting against changing its rules to accommodate so-called megacap IPOs like SpaceX's. A merger would open a different question of allowing the combined company to take over Tesla's S&P 500 slot or finding another company to replace it.

A spokesperson at S&P declined to comment, citing the firm's policy to not to discuss market speculation. Tesla and SpaceX did not reply to emails seeking comment.

The stakes are significant. The addition of the combined company could generate about $100 billion of demand for the stock from index funds, according to Reid Noch at TD Securities.

It could also ripple across the market more broadly by affecting the weightings of other companies in the index. Based on Friday's prices, Tesla and SpaceX have a combined stock-market value of nearly $3.5 trillion, which would make a combined firm the fifth biggest in the S&P 500.

"This one really raises the stakes," said Campbell Harvey, finance professor at Duke University. "This could soon be the largest company in the world, and it's difficult to make the case for it to be excluded from the most important index in the world."

Musk last month endorsed the idea of merging the two companies he runs and asked board members to consider it. People familiar with the matter said this week that a deal could be announced as soon as next month.

It's no sure thing that a Tesla-SpaceX would be added to the S&P 500, and if it isn't, passive investment funds would have to sell the shares they'd likely get in the combined company.

The easiest route in would be for Tesla to buy SpaceX, the larger of the two companies, though few expect a transaction to be structured that way.

But analysts say there's also a strong case for allowing the new company to keep Tesla's position even if the car company is the one that's acquired, because it would help the index preserve continuity and market representativeness while minimizing unnecessary turnover.

While SpaceX currently doesn't meet all the criteria for membership in the S&P 500 Index, which requires a stock to trade for at least a year and for the company to be profitable for the previous four combined quarters, it could clear that hurdle by the middle of next year, based on current analyst estimates.

The addition of a combined behemoth to the index would increase its sensitivity to tech stocks, which already have a heavier weighting in the benchmark than they did at the height of the dot-com boom. It's poised to get two new future contenders as Claude-owner Anthropic PBC stages its initial public offering and rival OpenAI is expected to follow next year.

"Our large cap indexes are moving a little bit more down the road of becoming effectively AI investment instruments," said Brent Leadbetter, head of RAFI distribution at TMX Group Ltd.'s VettaFi. "You're becoming more concentrated and that concentration brings risk."

data.title: Ray Dalio Says Mistakes Teach Life’s ‘Best Lessons’: Bitcoin Advocate Explains Why ‘Struggling Well’ Keeps ‘Bad Things’ Away
data.description:
Bridgewater Associates founder Ray Dalio once stressed the importance of learning from mistakes and turning struggles into growth.

Mistakes Happen in Pursuit of a Great Life, Says Dalio

On the Feb. 28, 2025 episode of The Foundr Podcast, the veteran investor said that life’s “best lessons” come from mistakes.

“You’re going to have struggles, and you’re going to make mistakes. Nobody skates through life, particularly if you want to have a great life,” Dalio emphasized.

He added that, when faced with a “painful result,” an individual should reflect on it objectively and seek advice from trusted people on how to handle a similar situation in the future.

How to Struggle Well?

Dalio grouped these habits under his broader philosophy of "struggling well."

“What I mean by struggle well is to know what your strengths and weaknesses are, to work with people who are strong,” he added.

Dalio compared life’s struggles to a tough workout, adding, "It gets you stronger. No pain, no gain. So if you can’t struggle well, you won’t stop the bad things coming at you.”

Dalio’s Path to Success

Dalio is the founder of Bridgewater Associates, currently the world’s biggest hedge fund, with assets under management of roughly $102 billion.

Today, with over 60 years of investing experience, Dalio’s fortune has grown to approximately $19 billion, according to Forbes.

Dalio has also written several bestselling books on economics, finance, and life philosophy, most notably “How Countries Go Broke: The Big Cycle.”

Dalio recommends a 1% Bitcoin allocation to navigate the risk of a debt crisis.

data.title: As Democrats seek changes to bill on energy permits, divisions emerge
data.description:
Key points:
  • House Democrats seek changes to bill that would streamline approvals for energy projects
  • Some Democrats argue for waiting rather than working with bipartisan bill in Senate now
  • Others say they should capitalize on current measure backed by Trump

By Valerie Volcovici

Democratic lawmakers in the US House of Representatives are working on changes to a sweeping energy permitting overhaul bill, but some of their colleagues want to wait until they take control of Congress next year.

The US Senate voted 73-25 last week to begin debate on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a far-reaching measure that would streamline approvals for power plants, transmission lines, mines and other projects while requiring large data centers to shoulder more of the costs of grid upgrades needed to serve them.

The legislation has exposed divisions among Democrats and environmental groups after midterm election results gave the Democratic Party majorities in both chambers of Congress next year.

Some Democrats have argued for waiting until they take over in January so they can pursue an ambitious package that does more to limit fossil fuel development.

Others say Congress should capitalize on the current bipartisan agreement moving through the Senate, particularly because President Donald Trump has indicated he would sign the measure.

"There's a lot of work behind the scenes right now to improve it," US Representative Kathy Castor, a Florida Democrat, told Reuters on the sidelines of the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.

Castor said she and other House Democrats are focused on revising provisions affecting the federal Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act rather than waiting for next year. She did not specify what changes they are seeking, but some Democratic lawmakers previously have expressed concerns that the Senate bill weakens some requirements for public input before projects are approved.

She praised measures already in the bill aimed at expanding transmission capacity, integrating more clean energy onto the grid, supporting community solar and establishing protections related to rapidly growing data center demand.

US Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, a Rhode Island Democrat, who is one of the bill's lead negotiators, told reporters in Antalya that he has received "good signals" from House colleagues that a compromise could be reached if the legislation clears the Senate in the coming weeks.

"I do think that success in the House depends on the continued support from the president ... and from a significant number of Democrats who support the bill," Whitehouse said.

While the measure has attracted support from Trump, organized labor and parts of the clean-energy industry, some Democrats who favor waiting until next year say that voters want both affordable energy and stronger safeguards to shape the expansion of data centers and the infrastructure needed to power them.

"Many of these senators and members of the House of Representatives were sent here by their voters to work on this very issue," US Representative Veronica Escobar, a Texas Democrat, told Reuters. "It's not like if we don't pass something now, it won't ever get done."

data.title: Google Launches Gemini 4 Hydrogen With 2.5x Faster Performance, Challenging GPT-6.1 and Claude
data.description:
Announced on November 12, the model brings a reported 2.5x improvement in task completion speed over Gemini 3.8 Flash, alongside stronger coding capabilities and lower execution costs. Google is positioning Hydrogen as an accessible option for developers and businesses that need fast AI execution without relying on its more computationally intensive models.

Google announced the global rollout of Gemini 4 Hydrogen, upgrading Search’s intent recognition to better understand complex, nuanced queries, including typos and natural language. Source: Google via X

The release also marks a significant expansion of Google's Gemini 4 ecosystem, with the model becoming available across Google Search, the Gemini app, AI Studio, and developer platforms. Its benchmark results place it ahead of GPT-6.1 Terra and Claude Sonnet 5.5 in several categories, although competitors retain advantages in other specialized tasks.

Gemini 4 Hydrogen Targets Faster AI Coding and Agentic Workflows

Google DeepMind designed Gemini 4 Hydrogen to handle everyday coding, software development, multimodal tasks, and agentic workflows with greater execution speed. Unlike Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon, which focus on complex reasoning and longer tasks, Hydrogen prioritizes rapid execution and efficiency.

Google introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen as a fast, efficient model for everyday coding, agentic workflows, and rapid execution, complementing Gemini 4 Carbon’s advanced reasoning capabilities. Source: Google AI via X

According to Google, Hydrogen completes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash at its default high thinking setting. The company also reported that its Terminal-Bench 4.1 score increased to 57%, compared with 18.2% for its predecessor.

The improvement extends beyond processing speed. Google said Hydrogen reduces fabricated claims by more than five times and handles unsuccessful tool calls or empty search results more effectively. These capabilities are particularly relevant to autonomous AI agents, which must navigate multiple steps, use external tools, and recover from errors without constant human intervention.

The model also introduces four configurable thinking levels, including a new xhigh setting. Users can adjust the reasoning effort according to the complexity of their tasks, balancing response speed against the resources required for more demanding work.

Google DeepMind said Hydrogen also surpassed Gemini 4 Argon on the Artificial Intelligence Index at its default high setting, scoring 51 against Argon's 50. Its score rises to 54 when using the highest xhigh setting.

Gemini 4 Hydrogen Challenges GPT-6.1 Terra and Claude Sonnet 5.5

Google's published benchmark evaluations show that Gemini 4 Hydrogen can compete with established frontier models across coding, reasoning, and professional workflows.

In the SWE-sweep evaluation, which measures an AI model's ability to identify and repair software issues, Hydrogen scored 13.5%. This exceeded Claude Sonnet 5.5 at 3.1% and GPT-6.1 Terra at 5.8%.

Google DeepMind introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen as a faster upgrade over Gemini 3.8 Flash, optimized for coding, multimodal tasks, agentic workflows, and everyday use. Source: @GoogleDeepMind via X

Hydrogen also recorded a 71.6% score on Agents' Last Exam v1.1, ahead of GPT-6.1 Terra at 69.8% and Claude Sonnet 5.5 at 60.4%. The benchmark evaluates how effectively AI systems complete complex professional tasks involving multiple steps and different forms of information.

Its HLE-Diamond score reached 58.8%, compared with 53.3% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 and 47.3% for GPT-6.1 Terra. On AutomationBench-AA, Hydrogen achieved 76.1%, outperforming both competitors in the published comparison.

However, the results do not establish an across-the-board advantage. Claude Sonnet 5.5 scored 63.9% on Terminal-Bench 4.1, above Hydrogen's 57%. Claude also led the OSWorld-2.1 computer-use evaluation with 83.9%, compared with Hydrogen's 77.6%.

Google's evaluation methodology combines its own testing with results reported by competing model providers and public benchmark leaderboards. The company also used different testing configurations across evaluations, making individual benchmark results more useful than treating the overall comparison as a definitive ranking.

Nevertheless, the results demonstrate Google's progress in making a faster model competitive across several demanding AI applications.

Independent Tests Highlight Gemini 4 Hydrogen's Cost Advantage

Early demonstrations from independent developers have also drawn attention to Hydrogen's execution speed and operating costs.

In one comparison shared by developer @EnvolDev, Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Carbon were assigned the same complex task through OpenRouter using the High setting. Hydrogen completed the task in 1 hour and 23 minutes at a reported cost of $4.27.

A split-screen video compares Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Carbon generating an arctic boat scene, highlighting Hydrogen’s faster execution and lower cost. Source: @EnvolDev/X

Gemini 4 Carbon took 2 hours and 39 minutes and cost $8.83 to complete the same task. The side-by-side demonstration showed both models generating an arctic boat scene with ice formations and marine elements.

Although this was an individual test rather than a standardized benchmark, the results highlight the potential cost and time advantages of using Hydrogen for workloads that do not require the deeper reasoning capabilities of Carbon.

A separate demonstration shared by @AI_Screening compared Gemini 4 Hydrogen, Carbon, and Argon in AI video generation. The models generated a stylized horse galloping across a savanna at sunset, allowing viewers to compare motion quality, environmental effects, and visual consistency.

Hydrogen delivered competitive animation quality in the demonstration while offering faster generation and lower costs. These results suggest that the model could provide an efficient option for certain multimodal creative workflows, although individual demonstrations do not establish consistent performance across different prompts and generation tasks.

Google Upgrades Search With Gemini 4 Hydrogen

Alongside the model launch, Google has introduced a significant upgrade to Google Search, integrating Gemini 4 Hydrogen to improve how the platform understands and responds to complicated queries.

The November 12 rollout allows Search to interpret more nuanced, multi-part questions, including requests written in natural language or containing difficult-to-understand typos. The system is designed to identify the user's intent more accurately rather than relying solely on individual keywords.

Google has also improved its query fan-out capabilities. The technology allows Search to explore several related subtopics simultaneously, connecting users with a wider selection of relevant websites and information sources.

The updated experience introduces more adaptive visual responses, including images, comparison tables, structured information, and custom tools. These features are intended to make complicated searches easier to understand without requiring users to navigate multiple pages manually.

Robby Stein, Google's vice president of product for Search, described the release as the biggest model upgrade to Search yet. He said the update would help users find relevant information through more intuitive and visually structured responses.

Google also highlighted improvements to language understanding across supported AI Mode languages, extending the upgraded search experience to users making queries in different languages.

The integration is particularly important for Google's broader AI strategy because it brings Gemini's reasoning and information-processing capabilities directly into one of the company's most widely used products.

Gemini 4 Hydrogen Expands Across Google's AI Ecosystem

Google is making Gemini 4 Hydrogen available across its consumer, developer, and enterprise platforms, increasing access to its latest AI capabilities.

Developers can use the model through the Gemini API, Google AI Studio, and Android Studio. Businesses can also access it through Gemini for business and supported enterprise tools, while general users can find Hydrogen in the Gemini app and Google Search.

A split-screen comparison evaluates Gemini 4 Hydrogen, Carbon (Medium), and Argon in generating a galloping horse scene, highlighting differences in motion quality, dust effects, and visual consistency. Source: @AI_Screening/X

Google is also introducing a multi-model approach through its Antigravity development platform. Its Orchestrator feature can dynamically switch between Gemini 4 Carbon and Hydrogen during a single session, assigning more complex reasoning tasks to Carbon and faster execution work to Hydrogen.

According to Google, this approach achieved near-Carbon task success rates on Terminal-Bench 4.0 while using 24% less quota and completing tasks 19% faster on average.

The model's API pricing is set at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens across its one-million-token context window. This gives developers a defined cost structure when integrating Hydrogen into applications and automated workflows.

By combining configurable reasoning, faster execution, and multi-model coordination, Google is targeting users who need to manage increasingly complex AI workloads without relying exclusively on its most resource-intensive systems.

Google's AI Competition Intensifies

The launch of Gemini 4 Hydrogen strengthens Google's position in an increasingly competitive AI market, where model performance is no longer measured solely by reasoning capabilities.

Speed, inference costs, coding accuracy, and the ability to complete multi-step tasks have become important factors for developers and businesses choosing AI systems. Google's latest release addresses these requirements while extending its Gemini technology into Search and everyday productivity tools.

Its benchmark performance against GPT-6.1 Terra and Claude Sonnet 5.5 provides evidence of progress in several categories, although differences in computer use and terminal-based tasks show that competitors remain competitive.

The introduction of Hydrogen also reflects a broader shift toward specialized AI models that can handle routine execution more efficiently while working alongside larger systems for demanding reasoning tasks.

As Google expands access to Gemini 4 Hydrogen, its ability to maintain benchmark performance while delivering measurable savings in execution time and costs will be an important factor in determining its adoption among developers, enterprises, and everyday users.

data.title: FAA Administrator Bedford warns comms system will "continue to break" without fix
data.description:
A decades-old, antiquated telecommunications system that federal air traffic controllers rely on will continue to have problems until it is properly funded and fully upgraded with modern equipment, according to FAA Administration Bryan Bedford.

"But let's not kid ourselves," he said at a Saturday news conference. "It will continue to break until we fix it."

He added that the transformation from copper to fiber across the ATC network is about 70% complete.

The legacy system is known as the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure , which is managed by L3Harris Technologies . Per the company, FTI covers "4,400 facilities, manages more than 29,000 services, and supports the safe operation of 45,000 daily flights across the National Airspace System."

An upgrade from copper wires to fiber that included a router change conducted by L3Harris is to blame for Friday's nationwide ground stop, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said.

He added that AT&T , Verizon , and Lumen Technologies are working with the FAA on a replacement for FTI. "But in the meantime, until I can build that, I'm stuck with L3Harris, who owns this network."

Bedford maintained that until a new system is completely operational, his agency will continue to maintain the old one. He lamented there isn't enough funding to even do that properly given that a $30B request from Duffy to Congress was reduced first by the House and even more by the Senate.

He noted that ~$12.5B has been spent on modernization efforts so far.

Duffy recently called on Congress to approve $50B in funding for ATC upgrades.

data.title: Charles Hoskinson Clashes With Angry ADA Holders Over Promises of Price Gains
data.description:
Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson says he never promised that ADA would rise. He made the remarks during a heated livestream with frustrated investors.

His comments come as ADA trades near multi-year lows, far below highs from previous cycles.

Hoskinson Says Cardano’s Roadmap Is Complete

Cardano’s roadmap is a five-era development plan that guided the network from launch to full decentralized governance. Each era added a core feature to the blockchain:

  • Byron (2017): Launched the Cardano network in September 2017.
  • Shelley (2020): Added staking in July 2020.
  • Goguen (2021): Brought smart contracts through the Alonzo hard fork.
  • Basho (2022): Focused on scaling with the Vasil upgrade.
  • Voltaire (2024): Introduced on-chain governance through the Chang hard fork.

The last step came in January 2025 with the Plomin hard fork. That upgrade gave ADA holders direct voting power over the network’s future.

“…The roadmap is done. My job is done with Cardano.” Hoskinson said during the livestream. He added that everything he promised to build now exists.

“I have no power over this ecosystem,” he said. He also pointed to Cardano’s millions of users and its self-governance. In his view, the network no longer depends on him.

Why Are Cardano Investors So Frustrated?

Much of the anger comes down to price. During the stream, one viewer claimed that Hoskinson had promised Cardano would overtake Bitcoin.

He said he would love for that to happen, but he never promised price gains. He also noted that ADA holders now choose their own leaders.

“…I love how you say my promise of having Cardano overtake Bitcoin. I never promised that. I said I’d love for it to happen… But you’re crazy when you say, ‘Oh, Charles promised that,’… I don’t promise price appreciation or people overturning things…,” Cardano founder noted.

The viewer later shared an old quote. In it, Hoskinson said he thinks Cardano will probably become the largest cryptocurrency. However, he stressed the word “think” and said he has taken the project as far as he can.

Moreover, he argued that no endpoint would satisfy investors who want him to pump their bags. A founder who stops at $3 defrauds buyers at $3, in his view.

Meanwhile, the numbers explain the frustration. According to BeInCrypto data, ADA trades near $0.1635, down 26.6% over the past month.

The token also trades roughly 94.7% below its all-time high of $3.09, reached in September 2021.

As a result, many holders remain deeply underwater.

data.title: Facing Backlash on Land, Data Centers Look to the Sea — WSJ
data.description:
By Jackie Snow

Data centers on land have attracted a lot of opposition. So in response, more companies have an alternative: What if data centers were placed on the ocean, or on some other body of water, instead?

The idea is still in the early stages. But as battles over where to build data centers intensify, developers are betting that offshore facilities could face less opposition from the public. They wouldn't be located in neighborhoods, and many of the proposed projects plan to generate electricity from waves or tidal power and use seawater for cooling, which could help alleviate fears about power and water consumption.

Whether those advantages can outweigh the challenges of running computers at sea is an open question. But that hasn't stopped announcements of new ocean data-center projects from piling up.

In May, Portland, Ore.-based Panthalassa, a startup backed by investors including Peter Thiel, raised $140 million to build giant steel structures, each 278 feet long, that would power artificial-intelligence computing with electricity generated from waves, while floating untethered in the Pacific Ocean.

In July, Scottish firm Mocean Energy announced plans to put AI servers on floats far out at sea, powered by waves and solar panels, cooled by the surrounding water and linked to shore by satellite.

And in October, Ocean Power Technologies of New Jersey and Stratum Holdings of Florida signed a nonbinding letter of intent to test whether Ocean Power's prototype buoys, powered mainly by waves, wind and solar, could run Stratum's AI infrastructure without a power cable to shore.

Other developers have different approaches. Massachusetts-based DeepGreen Holdings has applied for a federal permit to study putting a tidal-powered underwater data center on the seabed off Eastport, Maine, and filed a similar application for Alaska's Cook Inlet. Tidal power comes from the flow of water close to shore as tides rise and fall.

And Japan's Mitsui O.S.K. Lines says it wants to build a new vessel or convert an existing ship into a floating data center moored in a port, powered either from shore or by a separate power ship.

Early stages

Most of the projects are still in the early stages.

Panthalassa says it plans to test its next-generation data center later this year and begin commercial deployment in 2027. DeepGreen is still vetting turbine and equipment partners and hasn't put anything in the water yet, says Louis Wolfson, the company's managing member. And Mitsui O.S.K. Lines is weighing sites for its first ship-based data center, according to Shinichi Ogawa, who leads the effort.

Mocean, meanwhile, completed a 13-month test of its wave-powered energy system in the spring of 2024. It announced plans in July to put AI servers on the unit and is now seeking funds for a demonstration.

The company's prototype is based on wave-energy technology it has been working on for a decade to provide electricity to offshore oil-and-gas operators. It consists of a floating device that moves with the waves, with a generator driven directly by that motion and few parts to break, says Cameron McNatt, the company's co-founder and chief executive. The system was able to generate electricity from waves up to 40 feet during testing, McNatt says, adding that very small waves produced less power.

Mocean intends for each unit, or node, to deliver about 500 kilowatts of power to AI computers through a combination of wave power and solar panels. In the test, the unit produced about 10 kilowatts, the company says. Mocean envisions nodes being joined into groups that could supply up to 100 megawatts and be placed where waves run strong, such as Western Europe, the U.S. West Coast, Chile and Western Australia. McNatt says the goal is to reach a gigawatt of capacity in five years and 10 gigawatts in a decade.

On calm, cloudy days, batteries would provide backup power. From shore, the units would be nearly out of sight.

"They're really low profile, sitting close to the water," McNatt says. "They would basically be invisible."

Challenges at sea

Generating electricity is one of the biggest challenges floating data centers face at sea.Running subsea cables back to shore to transmit power could eat up a project's budget before a developer even has a chance to prove its concept works, says Bryson Robertson, director of the Institute for Integrated Energy Systems at the University of Victoria. That is why many of the recently announced floating-data-center projects seek to generate power on site.

Machines that drift freely, rather than being anchored to the seabed, avoid the cost of moorings but face a different problem. Storms can drag them away from their intended locations, and steering them back takes power that otherwise could run the computers, according to Robertson.

Seawater itself is a problem because the salt can corrode metal. "You put anything into seawater, and it starts failing immediately," says Michael Barnard, a climate-technology consultant.

Barnacles, minerals and microorganisms built up on submerged surfaces, clogging intake filters and coating the heat exchangers that cool the servers, Barnard says. Sending crews out to fix equipment add cost and complexity. He questions whether wave machines could be kept running reliably enough for the job.

Mocean says it plans to use marine-grade anti-corrosion paint and antifouling paint, a coating designed to stop marine life from attaching to vessels, when needed. And it will tow units back to a dock for scheduled repairs.

Wave-energy devices, meanwhile, cannot simply be built bigger to generate more power, says Robertson. They have to be tuned to the rhythm of the waves where they operate. A device that grows too large wouldn't be able to capture much of what the ocean actually produces. "It's like building a 500-meter-wide wind turbine, but there's never enough wind to make it spin," he says.

Then there are the environmental concerns. In Maine, groups opposing DeepGreen's plan say the Bay of Fundy is habitat for some of the world's most endangered whales. Moving data centers farther offshore isn't the answer because it would add boat traffic that raises the risk of whale strikes, along with noise that can interfere with how whales find food and mates, says Kristen Monsell, oceans program litigation director at the Center for Biological Diversity, which has filed to take part in the federal review. She also pointed to water pollution and heat.

DeepGreen's Wolfson says the purpose of the multiyear preliminary study is to examine such concerns, adding that the company is only reviewing turbine systems that operate within safe acoustic limits for marine mammals and fish. He also says DeepGreen plans to consult tribal leaders, fishermen and town officials before seeking a license.

Wave-energy projects aren't new and companies involved in this space have faced a high rate of failure over the years for a variety of reasons, including the harsh ocean environment and high costs.

Still, Robertson says deep-pocketed technology companies might finally give them the room to keep trying. "It's nice to see industries start to spend money in the wave-energy space," he says. "No technology works the first time."

Write to reports@wsj.com

data.title: SpaceX's Starship nears end of 15th test flight and return-landing attempt
data.description:
By Joey Roulette

SpaceX's next-generation Starship spacecraft cruised around the globe on Saturday nearing the end of its 15th test flight and what the company hoped would be an unprecedented pinpoint return landing at the exact spot in Texas from which it launched.

Starship's uncrewed upper stage is poised to re-enter Earth's atmosphere after nearly a day in orbit and steer back toward its launch tower, then make an engine-controlled final descent into the embrace of giant mechanical arms designed to catch the vehicle as it hovers over the launchpad.

If successful, it will mark the first round-trip voyage of a vertically launched spacecraft to orbit and back to the very spot where it left Earth, achieving a key test of Elon Musk's long-pursued goal of producing a fully reusable rocket system.

The towering two-stage rocket's Super Heavy booster - the rocket's bottom half - carried Starship to space on Friday, lifting off from SpaceX's Starbase, Texas facilities. That booster had failed to return to the launch pad some 10 minutes after liftoff because of an onboard navigation issue, nixing SpaceX's plan to recover both parts of the rocket for the first time.

Starship, cruising at an altitude of roughly 161 miles (260km), is expected to complete 14 orbits around Earth for a total flight time of 22 hours 32 minutes.

The 15th Starship flight since 2023 became the longest-lasting mission last night, lasting longer than the roughly three-hour trek in its 14th flight in September, when it reached orbit for the first time.

SpaceX has spent roughly a decade developing Starship, which billionaire CEO Elon Musk sees as the future workhorse for the company's satellite business and ambitions to put humans on the moon and eventually Mars.

SpaceX's dominance in the global launch industry has been centered on its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket, which has launched over 700 times since 2010. That rocket's first stage is reusable, but its second stage - the part that delivers payloads into orbit - is discarded into the ocean after each flight.

Starship's Super Heavy booster has been recovered on three previous test flights using the launch-tower catching system, the last such catch occurring in March 2025. The company has not made such a landing since, either because it planned to dunk it in the Gulf waters or because of an onboard glitch.

data.title: Bitcoin ETFs lose $1 billion for the second week in a row as crypto funds, except one, continue bleeding
data.description:
U.S. spot bitcoin (BTC) ETFs saw $1.07 billion in net outflows last week, their second straight week with more than $1 billion leaving the funds, per The Block's analysis of SoSoValue data. The last time the funds posted back-to-back $1 billion outflow weeks was in late May and early June.

The selling stretched to nearly every crypto ETF category. Of the 15 groups of U.S. spot crypto funds tracked by SoSoValue, 10 posted net outflows last week and four reported no flows at all. Avalanche (AVAX) funds were the only category with a weekly inflow, taking in a minute $227,000 on Thursday. Overall, U.S. spot crypto ETFs saw about $1.55 billion in total leave the funds.

The bitcoin funds saw outflows in all five days last week. They lost $201.1 million on Monday, $95 million on Tuesday, $299.9 million on Wednesday, $284 million on Thursday and $185.5 million on Friday.

Combined with the $1.28 billion that left the funds the week before, bitcoin ETFs have now shed $2.35 billion over two weeks. That is the largest two-week total since the fortnight ending June 5, when the funds lost $3.14 billion.

Bitcoin funds deepen 2026 losses with seven-day outflow streak

Friday's outflow was the bitcoin funds' seventh consecutive daily loss, a losing streak that has drained $1.91 billion from the funds since it began Nov. 5. It is the longest daily outflow streak since the 10-session stretch from June 17 to July 1, which drained about $2.71 billion, as The Block reported at the time.

BlackRock's IBIT accounted for $143.5 million of Friday's outflows, or about 77% of the total, per SoSoValue. Fidelity's FBTC lost $41.9 million, and the other 10 funds reported no flows. IBIT currently holds bitcoin worth $53.99 billion against $64.19 billion in cumulative inflows since launch.

Bitcoin ETFs have come to lose $2.35 billion in November after nine trading days, already their largest monthly outflow since June, when $4.51 billion left the funds. They are now down about $1.98 billion for 2026, more than double the $914.1 million deficit they carried a week earlier after flipping negative for the year.

The outflows came as bitcoin dropped below $69,000 early Friday, its lowest level since Aug. 20 at the time, as traders weighed Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO and expectations of another Federal Reserve rate hike, as The Block reported. The world's most valuable cryptocurrency fell further on Saturday morning, currently trading around $65,650, per The Block's Bitcoin price page.

Ether funds approach record outflow streak

Spot ether (ETH) ETFs lost $398.9 million last week, per SoSoValue, their seventh consecutive negative week; the category has twice posted eight-week outflow streaks, most recently when it matched that record in early July, so another negative week would tie it again.

The seven-week losing streak has pulled about $2.42 billion from the funds since late September, per SoSoValue's data. Monday's $184.5 million outflow was last week's largest, followed by $144.8 million on Wednesday and $70.6 million on Thursday.

A minuscule $2.4 million inflow on Friday ended a six-trading-day outflow streak worth $594.4 million. Fidelity's FETH drew $11.6 million that day, offsetting a $9.3 million outflow from Grayscale's Ethereum Mini Trust, while BlackRock's ETHA reported no flows.

Ether ETFs are now down about $804.5 million for 2026, nearly double the $405.6 million deficit from a week earlier. Net assets fell 15.5% over the week to $10.85 billion, their lowest since Aug. 18 and about $670 million below the funds' $11.52 billion in cumulative net inflows.

Altcoin funds extend outflows, save for one

Spot Solana ETFs lost $32.1 million last week, per SoSoValue, their sixth straight negative week and the longest such run since the funds launched in October 2025. The outflow streak began the same week the funds snapped a record 14-week inflow run, and it has drained $197.4 million since.

The Solana funds posted outflows in every session last week, extending their daily losing streak to seven days. Fidelity's FSOL accounted for all of Friday's $3.1 million outflow. Net assets fell to $1.14 billion from $1.31 billion a week earlier, though, unlike their BTC and ETH brethren, the funds remain about $644.1 million positive for the year.

Grayscale's Zcash fund, ZCSH, the only U.S. spot Zcash ETF, lost $30.7 million, nearly as much as the nine Solana funds combined, per SoSoValue. It was the fund's second straight negative week, and the outflow matched an early-October week as its largest since late September. ZCSH's net assets fell 32% over the week to $523.7 million.

Spot XRP ETFs shed $19.1 million, per SoSoValue, their largest weekly outflow since mid-March and a second straight negative week. Most of it left on Monday and Tuesday, at $10.4 million and $7.6 million, respectively. On Friday, Grayscale's GXRP lost $5.5 million while Franklin's XRPZ took in $4.5 million.

The three U.S. Hyperliquid ETFs lost $4.3 million, extending their weekly outflow streak to six, the longest since they began trading in May, per SoSoValue. Smaller funds tracking NEAR, Chainlink, Hedera and Polkadot lost between $99,000 and $1.4 million each. The BNB, Dogecoin, Tron and Litecoin funds reported no flows for the week.

The Avalanche funds’ modest $227,000 inflow on Thursday, their only day with any net flows, formed the only black in a sea of red last week.

data.title: Hot Wheels Crowns 2026 Legends Tour Winner Following Global Search Across 19 Countries
data.description:
Mattel, Inc. (), a leading global play and family entertainment company and owner of one of the world’s most iconic brand portfolios, today announced the 2026 winner of the Hot Wheels™ Legends Tour presented by Mobil 1, the world’s largest traveling car show and global custom car competition. At the November 14 Global Grand Finale, Matt McEntegart’s custom 1979 Chevrolet El Camino, which began its journey by winning the Tampa stop, was crowned the global champion. The victory marks the first time a U.S. entry has won the global title since 2022. The one-of-a-kind creation will now be inducted into the Hot Wheels Garage of Legends™ and transformed by the Hot Wheels® design team into an official 1:64-scale die-cast collectible sold worldwide.

This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261114608677/en/

Hot Wheels Crowns 2026 Legends Tour Winner Following Global Search Across 19 Countries

McEntegart’s custom 1979 Chevrolet El Camino, nicknamed the “SS Monte Mino,” combines elements of three iconic Chevrolet vehicles: the El Camino, Monte Carlo SS and sixth-generation Corvette. Built over thousands of hours, the project involved mounting the El Camino body onto a modified 2008 Corvette chassis and stretching the wheelbase by 12 inches. Reflecting the creativity, authenticity and garage spirit of the Hot Wheels Legends Tour, McEntegart designed and fabricated nearly every aspect of the vehicle himself. The process involved shaping foam prototypes, creating molds and fabricating a custom Monte Carlo-inspired widebody, finished in rich maroon paint with red-tinted forged carbon fiber panels that capture the distinctive styling of a Hot Wheels car.

Beneath its custom hood, the El Camino features a modified Chevrolet V8 engine with exposed velocity stacks and several performance upgrades. A custom air suspension system allows the vehicle to sit exceptionally low over massive 22-inch wheels. Inside, the bespoke cabin blends retro 1980s styling with modern Corvette technology, featuring custom upholstery and interior components handcrafted by McEntegart.

Ted Wu, General Manager and Global Head of Vehicles and Building Sets at Mattel, said: “What makes Hot Wheels Legends Tour so special is its ability to bring automotive communities together and celebrate the incredible talent of builders around the world. Matt’s El Camino stood out for its bold design and craftsmanship, and we’re honored to turn his passion project into an official Hot Wheels die-cast car for fans to play and collect around the world.”

The 2026 Hot Wheels Legends Tour traveled to 19 countries, including 12 stops across North America, bringing together thousands of custom vehicles from around the world. Hot Wheels designers and local automotive experts evaluated entries based on authenticity, creativity and garage spirit. Winners from local Tour stops advanced to their respective regional finals, with champions from North America, Europe, Middle East and Africa (EMEA), Latin America (LATAM) and Asia-Pacific (APAC) competing in the Global Grand Finale, where McEntegart ultimately took home the top honor.

The 2026 Hot Wheels Legends Tour runners-up included Sandranto Hertanu, aka Achun Owen, of Indonesia, Andrea Cionco of Italy and Andres Romero Maureira of Chile. Hertanu transformed a 1961 Morris Mini Van into a custom pickup, while Cionco reimagined a 1990 Mazda MX-5 NA with Japanese-inspired widebody styling. Romero Maureira rounded out the finalists with his 1992 Chevrolet Salaya SP, a purpose-built race car powered by a 450-horsepower V8 engine.

Since its launch in 2018 to celebrate Hot Wheels’ 50th anniversary, the Hot Wheels Legends Tour presented by Mobil 1 has grown from a U.S.-based series of local Walmart events into the world’s largest traveling car show and global custom car competition, attracting builders and automotive fans through live and virtual events. Previous champions include the inaugural 2018-winning 2JetZ™, 2019-winning THE NASH™, 2020-winning 1970 Pontiac® Firebird™, 2021-winning 1969 Volvo P1800 Gasser, 2022-winning “Texas Toot,” an ultra-custom 1992 Autozam Scrum micro truck, 2023-winning 1990 Mazda MX-5 roadster nicknamed “Chimera,” 2024-winning custom-built 1968 Ford Falcon nicknamed “La Liebre,” and 2025-winning rally-inspired Fiat 126P Bis from Poland.

To learn more about the Hot Wheels Legends Tour, visit www.HotWheels.com/Legends.

About Mattel

Mattel is a leading global play and family entertainment company and owner of one of the most iconic brand portfolios in the world. We engage consumers and fans through our franchise brands, including Barbie®, Hot Wheels®, Fisher-Price®, American Girl®, Thomas & Friends™, UNO®, Masters of the Universe®, Matchbox®, Monster High®, Polly Pocket®, as well as other popular properties that we own or license in partnership with global entertainment companies. Our offerings include toys, content, consumer products, digital and live experiences. Our products are sold in collaboration with the world’s leading retail and ecommerce companies. Since its founding in 1945, Mattel is proud to be a trusted partner in empowering generations to explore the wonder of childhood and reach their full potential. Visit us at mattel.com.

An investment firm connecting emerging and developed markets. And a software company turning every internet connection into a media business. These are the stories our audience in every region tunes in for. No politics. No current events. Only Opportunities To Consider™."

INSIDE SHOW #780

Robo.ai Inc. : Where Global AI Investment Meets Local Capability

In a three-executive panel, Jane King asks where Robo.ai fits in the AI investment cycle. Ralf R. Debbas, President of Robo.ai, describes the company as a UAE-based, Nasdaq-listed group "connecting regional technology with global market reach."

He outlines its main operating businesses: Neurovia AI, focused on visual data efficiency; ALIF Holding, which brings industrial integration, manufacturing and execution; and Quantum Core Capital (QC Capital), which contributes operating revenue and is developing AI applications including AI-generated video and content creation.

"Our ambition is to help build sovereign AI capabilities within the UAE itself and the wider region," Debbas said, "technology that can be deployed, supported and developed locally."

Dr. Jasem Al Mansoori, Chief Executive Officer of ALIF Holding, Robo.ai's Abu Dhabi-based industrial group, draws on more than 30 years at the UAE Ministry of Interior. "This experience taught me the importance of reliable solutions and strong local support," he said. ALIF is developing an industrial base in the UAE for engineering and manufacturing, and aims to use AI to help industrial customers work more efficiently and make better decisions.

Mansoor Ali Khan, Chief Technology Officer of Neurovia AI, explains why efficiency matters as AI computing competition intensifies and memory and storage costs rise. Khan notes that the large majority of the world's data is visual and unstructured.

Neurovia's flagship NeuroStream™ platform is designed to reduce the volume of visual data that is transmitted, processed and stored. In a company demonstration shown on air, a 12.15 GB 4K video file was reduced to 421 MB, a reduction of more than 96%. Khan said the goal is to address the main costs of AI (storage, compute, transmission and power) and make AI "more affordable and sustainable." Actual results depend on deployment conditions and use-case validation.

Learn more at roboai.group.

American Fusion Inc. : Independent Review, a New Texas Campus and a Busy Six Months

Chairman and CEO Brent Nelson returns to update Jane King on American Fusion's Texatron™ aneutronic fusion engine. Nelson says an independent third-party reviewer recently completed an on-site evaluation of the technology, with a final report expected later this month. "The draft highlights look good so far," he said, adding that the company hopes the report will confirm "that we're on the right track."

Nelson, who added the CEO title in late October, says his priorities for the next six months include closing on the company's North Texas "Ranch" facility, which American Fusion expects by Thanksgiving, and developing the property. The company is also moving from its temporary facility into new lab and office space, and plans to build its own testing bunker at the Ranch. "We're still operating and testing the Texatron on a daily basis," Nelson said, "and our data is getting better."

He also says the company's patent program remains active, with new applications being written daily, and that its data center proposals are moving forward.

Learn more at americanfusionenergy.com.

Stewards Investment Capital CEO Bilal Adam on Global Investing, Private Credit and Financial Inclusion

Bilal Adam, Chief Executive Officer of Stewards Investment Capital, joins Jane King to discuss the firm's international investment approach, private credit solutions and commitment to financial inclusion. A chartered accountant from South Africa with a background in investment banking, Adam describes building a business with activities spanning South Africa, Mauritius, the United States and Monaco.

Adam discusses the firm's investment philosophy, which he says starts with "aiming to do good first," and its relationship with Nasdaq-listed Stewards, Inc. , a U.S.-based diversified financial platform led by President and CEO Shaun Quin, which provides financing to small businesses across the United States. Stewards Investment Capital is affiliated with, but separate from, Stewards, Inc. He also highlights telecommunications tower investments aimed at expanding connectivity and financial inclusion in rural African communities.

The conversation explores how Stewards Investment Capital provides pension funds, institutions, family offices and high-net-worth investors with access to private credit, portfolio diversification and international investment opportunities, including a private credit approach that funds fractional amounts of loans to small businesses.

Learn more at stewardsinvestment.com.

FreeCast, Inc. : "The Connection Is Just the Beginning"

Founder and CEO William Mobley explains why FreeCast is "not another streaming service." Instead, the company provides the software infrastructure that lets telecom companies, wireless carriers, internet providers, satellite companies and membership organizations launch their own branded entertainment hubs, offering free television, premium subscriptions, sports, advertising and commerce. "They bring the customers," Mobley said. "We bring the media and monetization technology."

Mobley walks through PEAC, FreeCast's metric for "partner-enabled addressable customers," which measures potential distribution reach through enterprise agreements. He is clear that PEAC does not represent active users, paying subscribers or confirmed revenue. He describes the company's job as converting that reach into activated users, transactions and, ultimately, revenue across advertising, subscriptions, pay-per-view, live sports, rentals and commerce.

"We don't need Netflix to lose for FreeCast to succeed," Mobley said. "We want more content and more services participating in our marketplaces."

Learn more at freecast.com.

FEATURED COMMERCIALS

  • T-REX Acquisition Corp. : Completed a strategic refinancing of its Orofino, Idaho data center and added a new appointment to its board of directors.

The CM further recalled that the country's literacy rate was only 12 per cent, and the population encountered severe hardships due to food shortages in the initial times of Independent India.

He added that the then-Prime Minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, prioritised the sectors of education and irrigation, and laid the foundations for prestigious institutions like IIT Kharagpur. The economic reforms introduced by PV Narasimha Rao provided a new direction for the nation.

Reiterating that his government continued to uphold the positive policies implemented by the previous administrations of Chandrababu Naidu, Y.S. Rajasekhara Reddy, and KCR, the Chief Minister said that his government remains committed to continuing policies that foster development even despite political differences.

data.title: Novo's Wegovy pill helps patients lose about 6% of weight in three months, real-world data show
data.description:
By Patrick Wingrove

Patients who stayed on Novo Nordisk's daily Wegovy pill lost an average of 6.2% of their body weight over three months, according to real-world data due to be presented at the ObesityWeek conference in Washington.

The pill, launched in January, has helped Novo regain some ground lost to Eli Lilly , and the Danish drugmaker is trying to stay ahead of its US rival in the race for oral obesity treatments.

Novo's Chief ​Scientific Officer Martin Holst Lange said in an interview that the real-world data was encouraging as it broadly replicated the findings of 5.5% weight loss at 12 weeks seen in Novo's late-stage trial for the pill.

Study participants, who started taking the pill between January 5 and February 7, 2026, lost an average of 6.3 kg (13.9 pounds) from a baseline weight of 103.0 kg (227 pounds), Novo said. About three-fifths lost at least 5% of their weight, and roughly one in six lost at least 10%.

The analysis covered 5,872 adults on the Ro telehealth platform who had never taken a weight-loss drug and who stayed on the pill for the full three months.

Novo Nordisk's fortunes have declined significantly since it became Europe's most valuable listed company following the 2021 launch of its injectable weight-loss drug, Wegovy. Its stock has plummeted over 70% from its peak as Lilly surpassed it to take the lead in the obesity-drug market.

According to company presentations earlier this month, however, oral treatments now represent roughly a third of US obesity prescriptions, with Novo securing over 80% of new oral prescriptions.

The company in September said separate real-world data showed patients who switched from weight-loss injections to Novo's pill continued to lose weight.

Oral Wegovy — known chemically as semaglutide — led to about a 14% reduction in body weight over 64 weeks, while Eli Lilly's obesity pill Foundayo led to about an 11% reduction over 72 weeks, separate studies have shown.

data.title: Strategy's Michael Saylor proposes $10B-$30B digital credit plan
data.description:
Strategy has spent years buying Bitcoin with two tools: selling new common shares and benefiting from a rising Bitcoin price. On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, Executive Chairman Michael Saylor said the company may no longer need either one.

His pitch is that Strategy could create between $10 billion and $30 billion in what it calls "digital credit," backed by the balance sheet it already has. For a company whose whole identity is "buy more Bitcoin," that changes how the shopping gets funded.

Saylor described the $10 billion to $30 billion range as financing capacity. It would not require new common-stock issuance or any further gains in Bitcoin's price.

The $30 billion figure reflects the company's view of its own financial structure and Bitcoin holdings. It is not a fundraising target the company plans to hit immediately.

CEO Phong Le filled in the mechanics. He said the main way Strategy will acquire more Bitcoin going forward is by issuing preferred securities, particularly perpetual preferred shares such as STRC.

Perpetual preferred shares sit between bonds and common stock. Holders get a fixed dividend and stand ahead of common shareholders in line. They don't get voting power, and the shares have no maturity date. STRC is designed to pay double-digit yields and to work as a steadier alternative to holding Bitcoin directly.

As of October 25, 2026, Strategy held 848,517 BTC. That stack is up 26% for the year.

The company also reported about $5.07 billion in dollar assets. By Strategy's math, that reserve could cover preferred dividends and debt interest for roughly 3.4 years.

Strategy reported third-quarter net income of $19.53 billion, driven largely by a $20.91 billion gain on its digital assets.

Strategy already has a sizeable presence in this market. It currently has $16 billion in notional digital credit securities outstanding across ten listed instruments. The top end of Saylor's new range would be larger than everything it has issued in this category so far.

Strategy started as a traditional software company and has turned into one of the most prominent names among corporate Bitcoin treasuries.

The company now describes its capital approach in layers: digital capital, digital equity and digital credit. Bitcoin is the base layer. Common stock is the equity layer. The preferred instruments are the credit layer that the company now wants to lean on hardest.

The move also signals a step away from two funding sources that defined its earlier buying sprees: at-the-market (ATM) equity sales and convertible debt. ATM programs let a company sell shares into the market gradually. Preferred shares sidestep some of those issues. They don't add common shares, and perpetual instruments never come due. The trade-off is a standing dividend obligation that has to be paid regardless of where Bitcoin trades.

For common shareholders, the most obvious appeal is less dilution. If preferred issuance replaces ATM sales as the main funding channel, existing holders may see their ownership stretched less with each Bitcoin purchase. Their claim, however, sits behind a growing stack of preferred holders who get paid first.

For preferred buyers, the proposition is yield backed by a large Bitcoin position and a multi-year cash reserve. The 3.4-year coverage estimate is based on current obligations. Adding billions in new preferred paper would raise the annual dividend bill.

The reported earnings also deserve care from this group. A $19.53 billion quarter driven by a $20.91 billion digital-asset gain shows how directly Strategy's results follow Bitcoin.

data.title: Jensen Huang spy scandal puts Howard Lutnick in focus after Scott Bessent's remarks: What are his family's Nvidia ties?
data.description:
New Delhi, Nov. 14 -- US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has put Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick under fresh scrutiny over the Trump administration's handling of suspected Nvidia chip smuggling to China. Lutnick's family business ties to Nvidia and its AI partners have added another layer to the controversy.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's remarks about the handling of suspected Nvidia chip smuggling to China have brought Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick into the spotlight. Bessent said several government departments had supported placing Singapore-based Megaspeed on a restricted entity list for months, pointing to the Commerce Department as the agency responsible for taking action.

The comments have renewed attention on Lutnick's former Wall Street firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, which is now run by his sons, Brandon and Kyle Lutnick. The firm has reported investments in Nvidia and helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for companies connected to the chipmaker's artificial intelligence business.

There is no evidence that the family's business interests influenced Lutnick's government decisions or that his sons received confidential intelligence.

Before joining Donald Trump's administration in February 2025, Lutnick headed Cantor Fitzgerald. He later transferred his ownership stake to his children through trusts.

A CNBC analysis of securities filings found that Cantor's reported Nvidia shareholding fell by nearly 50% between September 2025 and March 2026.

At the end of 2024, the firm disclosed more than 3.5 million Nvidia shares worth approximately $479 million. Their value climbed to $652 million by September 2025. However, the reported share count fell to three million in December and 1.78 million by March 2026.

Cantor has not publicly explained the reduction. It has said the Nvidia positions reported in regulatory filings largely reflected client swap transactions rather than substantial standalone investments.

The controversy goes beyond Cantor's investments. According to Axios, Lutnick received a highly classified intelligence warning about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's alleged links to a suspected Chinese spy.

The Commerce Secretary also faced pressure from White House and intelligence officials to take action against Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company suspected of helping channel Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China.

Axios reported that Lutnick repeatedly resisted efforts to crack down on the company, despite Trump authorising fresh export restrictions.

Bessent's comments have exposed divisions within the administration over the issue. He said the Treasury, Defence and State departments, along with the US Trade Representative's office, had supported placing Megaspeed on the restricted entity list for months.

Cantor's business connections extend beyond its reported Nvidia shareholding.

In September, the firm hosted Huang and other senior Nvidia executives at investor meetings in New York. Its analysts subsequently maintained an overweight rating on Nvidia shares, describing the chipmaker as an attractive investment.

The firm has also helped finance companies in Nvidia's AI ecosystem.

In May 2026, Nvidia announced a five-year cloud computing agreement worth $3.4 billion with Australian company IREN. Days later, IREN announced a $3 billion convertible bond offering, with Cantor among seven banks arranging the deal.

Cantor also advised AI infrastructure developer Lancium on a $600 million financing deal for its data centre campus in Abilene, Texas. The project is connected to Stargate, the AI infrastructure initiative backed by OpenAI, SoftBank and Oracle.

The overlap between Lutnick's government responsibilities and his family's financial connections has attracted attention from ethics experts and lawmakers.

Richard Painter, a former White House chief ethics lawyer under George W Bush, told CNBC there was no proof Lutnick had shared confidential information with Cantor Fitzgerald. However, he said the appearance of a potential conflict was concerning.

Democratic lawmakers have also called for greater scrutiny of whether the Lutnick family could benefit from the administration's AI infrastructure policies.

The White House continues to back Lutnick. An official told Reuters that Trump retains complete confidence in the Commerce Secretary.

So far, there is no evidence that Lutnick's sons had advance knowledge of intelligence warnings about Huang or that Cantor's business interests influenced government decisions.

The Man Who Tells Corporate America How to Sell Stuff to Baby Boomers — WSJ
data.description:
By Rachel Louise Ensign | Photography by Ian Tuttle for WSJ

CHICAGO — Ken Dychtwald sat on stage in front of a ballroom of hundreds of people who work in the senior-housing industry.

Tan and fit in a black T-shirt and gray suit, he told the audience that their prospective residents will soon be the individualistic and high-maintenance baby boomers. "Get ready for the complaining," Dychtwald said to audience laughter. "Get ready for the demands."

Dychtwald has been predicting the ascendance of aging boomers for decades as a public speaker and boardroom consultant. Now the moment the 76-year-old has long forecast is here.

Selling things to older people was once an afterthought for companies. That has started to change in recent decades as the population aged. The boomer generation's massive size, high levels of wealth and desire to spend freely are making these customers even more desirable.

This generation collectively has far more money than any other group. According to the Federal Reserve, boomers currently hold more than $97 trillion in wealth, more than twice as much as the next-richest generation, Gen X. In the past year alone, boomers gained $12 trillion in wealth.

Dychtwald got his start in California's New Age scene. A fan of science fiction, he has tried predicting what the world would look like with the boomers as the most consequential group of older consumers yet. In a 1989 book, one of 19 he has written, he wrote that "the coming 'age wave' will challenge and shake every aspect of our personal, social and political dynamics."

Top executives started turning to Dychtwald for advice selling to the graying population. He advised Chrysler Chief Executive Lee Iacocca that the then-middle-age boomers would want to drive minivans. Dychtwald said he also played a role in the development of products including Michelob Ultra, multivitamin Centrum Silver, and Tylenol's arthritis product. He helped former President Jimmy Carter write a book.

Financial advisory firm Edward Jones hired Dychtwald in 2019. He worked with pollsters to survey thousands of people about retirement, finding that boomers increasingly saw retirement not as a time for rest but as a time for reinvention and exploration.

Dychtwald and Edward Jones dubbed their priorities — health, family, purpose and finances — the four "life pillars." The investment company trademarked the term, and its advisers now use the concept to guide conversations with their clients.

"It put words to something that they never had words for before," said Ken Cella, head of external affairs at Edward Jones. Dychtwald has done six more surveys for the company.

The Age Wave

Dychtwald grew up in a middle-class family in Newark, N.J., where his father owned area clothing stores. He left college, where he was studying to be an engineer, to move to California. He spent years regularly visiting the Esalen Institute in Big Sur, where nudity was common. Dychtwald got a Ph.D. in psychology and fashioned his dissertation on the mind-body connection as a book.

He started working with elderly people in his 20s when he helped run a program using yoga and meditation to improve their health. He eventually started his own company, Age Wave, to help companies understand the older demographic. Dychtwald learned about his subject by talking to older people and working with mentors including elderly-rights activist Maggie Kuhn. He once hired a professor to teach him about what it was like to be old throughout history.

In the 1990s, television network CBS was struggling to land advertisers because its viewers skewed older. They hired Dychtwald, who arranged meetings to persuade prospective advertisers these viewers were worth targeting. Those meetings yielded $600 million in new ad spending the following year, said Joe Abruzzese, who ran ad sales at CBS at the time. "He's probably the best speaker I've ever seen," Abruzzese said.

Dychtwald started building companies with products that catered to older people, such as local magazines and a health-products superstore. It gave him what he said was a net worth of more than $25 million. Those all unraveled right before the dot-com bubble burst, leaving him broke and contemplating suicide.

Eventually, he rebuilt his business. Now it has five employees, including his wife of 43 years, Maddy Dychtwald, who is also a speaker on aging.

'This Has Never Happened Before'

These days, Dychtwald spends much of his time doing interviews and giving speeches, where his going rate is $60,000. Two years ago, he addressed the Business Council, made up of CEOs of the largest U.S. companies. He does about half of his 15 or so keynote speeches a year now free to nonprofits.

Despite his decades in California, he retains an East Coast intensity. When audience members tell him they enjoyed his talk, he counters: "What about it was great?"

Talking about seniors is different now that Dychtwald is one himself. "I profoundly underestimated how painful it is to lose a loved one or how frightening it is to have your body start to fail," he said in an interview.

Both of his parents lived into their 90s, but with long declines — his mother had Alzheimer's disease and his father went blind from macular degeneration. Dychtwald estimates he spent around $1 million on home healthcare for them. Two of his friends died in recent months.

Dychtwald eats an anti-inflammatory diet, exercises twice a day, takes about a dozen different vitamins and gets regular massages. He has no plans to ever stop working.

He thinks companies are doing a much better job at catering to older Americans these days. High-end cruise lines are offering ambitious itineraries to curious older travelers. Home Depot hires elderly people for part-time jobs. Mercedes-Benz sells models that make it easier to get in and out, but doesn't pitch them explicitly to seniors. "They know their audience is older, but they don't hammer on it," he said. (These companies aren't currently clients).

Decades ago, Dychtwald predicted America would turn into a "gerontocracy," where economic and political power shifted from the young to the old. Dychtwald thinks politicians will start saying that boomers have too many resources. "We've made it really hard to be young," he said.

After decades of speeches, Dychtwald is closely attuned to his audience. At the October National Investment Center for Seniors Housing and Care conference, he asked people to raise a hand if they would like to live to 100. About half did, a likely testament to the group's familiarity with the dark side of growing old.

He called on audience members. "It's more about healthspan than lifespan," one said, referencing the buzzy idea that healthy years are what's most important. "Oh, there's great words," Dychtwald replied.

Dychtwald put up a slide with some stark demographic data. It showed the population of Americans 65 and over set to skyrocket, while all other age groups will grow slowly or even decrease. "Holy moly are you in the right places right now," he told the attendees about their line of work. "This has never happened before."

That compliment came with a grain of salt. Dychtwald suggested the industry might consider changing its name altogether. He showed a picture of Tom Cruise starring in the "Top Gun" sequel as an example of the new ideal. "I've looked at every study in the last 10 years. Boomers don't ever want to be a 'senior,'" he said. "I know that this is 'senior housing' and that worked. It may not work going forward."
